essentials: The CSDDD obliges very large companies to **look for, prevent and remedy** harm to people and the environment in their own operations, their subsidiaries and their chain of activities.
After **Omnibus I** it covers companies with **more than 5,000 employees and more than €1.5bn turnover**, including non-EU companies with that turnover in the EU.
It is an obligation of **means**, not of results: a company must take appropriate measures, not guarantee a harm-free supply chain.
Member States must transpose it by **26 July 2028**; obligations are expected to apply from **July 2029**.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: Voluntary standards for responsible business conduct have existed for years: the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines. Some Member States turned them into law, notably France (2017) and Germany (2021), each differently. The CSDDD, adopted in 2024, creates one EU framework so that large companies face the same expectations across the single market and affected people have a route to remedy.
It is the counterpart to the CSRD. The CSRD asks companies to **report** on sustainability; the CSDDD asks them to **act**.

after: Smaller companies are not directly bound, but they are part of the chains of in-scope companies and will be asked for information and commitments. The directive limits what can be passed down to them.

sections.title: The due diligence process
text: The directive turns the international due diligence cycle into legal duties.
steps: **Embed**: adopt a due diligence policy and a code of conduct, and integrate them into management systems.
**Identify and assess**: map where adverse impacts are most likely and most severe, then examine those areas in depth.
**Prioritise**: where not everything can be addressed at once, deal with the most severe and most likely impacts first.
**Prevent and mitigate** potential impacts: action plans, contractual assurances, support for suppliers, changes to purchasing practices.
**Bring actual impacts to an end** or minimise them, and **provide remediation** where the company caused or jointly caused the harm.
**Engage with stakeholders** such as workers, communities and their representatives at defined points of the process.
**Run a complaints procedure** open to affected people and organisations.
**Monitor** whether the measures work and **communicate** publicly, through the CSRD statement where the company reports under it.

sections.title: What ‘adverse impact’ and ‘chain of activities’ mean
points: **Adverse impacts** are defined by reference to an annex of international conventions: human rights such as the prohibition of child labour and forced labour, safe working conditions, freedom of association and a living wage, and environmental obligations on topics such as biodiversity, hazardous chemicals and waste.

The **chain of activities** covers the upstream partners involved in producing goods or providing services, direct and indirect, and a limited part of the downstream chain: distribution, transport and storage carried out for the company. The use of products by customers and the financial services of banks to their clients are outside.

sections.title: What Omnibus I changed
points: **Risk-based approach**: companies start from a general scoping exercise using reasonably available information and go into depth only where severe impacts are most likely. Systematic questionnaires to every business partner are not required.
**Protection of smaller partners**: information may be requested from smaller business partners only where it is necessary and cannot reasonably be obtained otherwise.
**No climate transition plan**: the duty to adopt and implement a plan aligned with the Paris Agreement was deleted.
**Civil liability**: the harmonised EU liability regime was removed. Liability follows national law, and Member States must still ensure access to remedy.
**Penalties**: capped at 3% of net worldwide turnover.
**Timing**: transposition moved to 26 July 2028, application to July 2029.

sections.title: Enforcement
text: Each Member State designates a supervisory authority that can investigate, order a company to act and impose fines. Authorities cooperate in a European network. Injured parties can bring claims under national law. Commission guidelines are due before the rules apply and will matter for how ‘appropriate measures’ is read.

terms.text: A continuous process to identify, prevent, mitigate, end and remedy adverse impacts, and to account for how this is done.
Harm to human rights or the environment resulting from a breach of the rights and prohibitions listed in the annex.
Upstream business partners plus downstream distribution, transport and storage. Narrower than the ‘value chain’ of the CSRD.
Measures capable of achieving the objective, proportionate to the severity and likelihood of the impact and reasonably available to the company.
A company with which the in-scope company has a commercial agreement (direct), or which performs activities connected to its operations without one (indirect).
A duty to make appropriate efforts. The company is not liable merely because harm occurred somewhere in its chain.
Restoring affected people or the environment to the situation before the harm, or as close as possible, including compensation.

related.text: The reporting side. Companies under both directives report on their due diligence through the sustainability statement.
Product-specific due diligence for seven commodities, with far more detailed evidence requirements than the CSDDD.
A product ban, not a process duty. Sound CSDDD due diligence is the best protection against a ban.
An older, sector-specific due diligence regime for four minerals, built on the same OECD guidance.

The Taxonomy's minimum safeguards point to the same international standards.

mistakes.wrong: A company is liable for every violation in its supply chain.
mistakes.right: The duty is to take appropriate measures. Liability arises where the company failed in that duty and thereby caused or contributed to harm, under national law.

mistakes.wrong: The CSDDD still requires a climate transition plan.
mistakes.right: Omnibus I deleted that obligation. Reporting on an existing plan can still be required under the CSRD.

mistakes.wrong: Due diligence means auditing every supplier.
mistakes.right: The approach is risk-based: scope broadly with available information, then focus on where severe harm is most likely.

mistakes.wrong: Companies below the thresholds can ignore the directive.
mistakes.right: They will face contractual requirements from in-scope customers, within the limits the directive sets.

mistakes.wrong: Ending the business relationship is the expected reaction to a problem.
mistakes.right: Engagement comes first. Disengagement is a last resort, because walking away often leaves affected people worse off.

practice: **Confirm scope** at group level and identify the Member State whose authority would supervise you.
**Run the scoping exercise**: map operations, subsidiaries and chain of activities, and mark sectors and countries with elevated risk.
**Go deep where risk is high** and document why other areas were not prioritised.
**Review purchasing practices**: prices, lead times and order changes are a common root cause of harm at suppliers.
**Set up or upgrade the complaints procedure** so that workers and communities in the chain can reach you.
**Align with existing duties**, such as the German Supply Chain Act, until national law is replaced by the transposition.

quiz.q: Which companies are covered by the CSDDD after Omnibus I?
options: More than 1,000 employees and €450m turnover
More than 5,000 employees and more than €1.5bn turnover
More than 250 employees in high-risk sectors
All companies importing into the EU
quiz.why: Omnibus I raised both thresholds. The 1,000 / €450m thresholds are now those of the CSRD.

quiz.q: What kind of obligation is due diligence under the CSDDD?
options: An obligation to guarantee that no harm occurs in the chain
An obligation to take appropriate measures
An obligation to publish a list of suppliers
An obligation to obtain a certificate for every supplier
quiz.why: It is an obligation of means. Companies must make appropriate, proportionate efforts.

quiz.q: What happened to the climate transition plan obligation?
options: It was strengthened
It was postponed to 2030
It was deleted by Omnibus I
It was moved to the Taxonomy Regulation
quiz.why: The duty to adopt and put into effect a transition plan was removed from the CSDDD.

quiz.q: Which part of the downstream chain is included in the ‘chain of activities’?
options: The use of products by consumers
Distribution, transport and storage for the company
The disposal of products at end of life
All customers of the company
quiz.why: Downstream coverage is limited to distribution, transport and storage. Product use and disposal are outside.

quiz.q: What is the cap on fines after Omnibus I?
options: 1% of EU turnover
3% of net worldwide turnover
5% of net worldwide turnover
There is no cap
quiz.why: Omnibus I set the cap at 3% of net worldwide turnover.

quiz.q: A company finds a serious labour rights problem at a supplier. What does the directive expect first?
options: Immediate termination of the contract
Engagement to prevent, mitigate or end the impact, with disengagement as a last resort
A report to the European Commission
Nothing, if the supplier is outside the EU
quiz.why: The directive favours staying and fixing the problem. Ending the relationship can harm the affected workers further.

quiz.q: By when must Member States transpose the CSDDD?
options: 19 March 2027
26 July 2027
26 July 2028
1 January 2030
quiz.why: Omnibus I moved the transposition deadline to 26 July 2028, with application expected a year later.

quiz.q: How do the CSDDD and the CSRD relate?
options: The CSDDD replaced the CSRD
The CSDDD requires action on impacts; the CSRD requires reporting
Both apply only to financial institutions
The CSRD applies only where the CSDDD does not
quiz.why: They are complementary: one sets a duty of conduct, the other a duty of transparency, and the report is where due diligence is communicated.
